samples.text:
Nowadays, most people get their news from the internet instead of reading newspapers or watching television. This change has both advantages and disadvantages.

The main advantage of online news is that it is fast. When something important happen in the world, people can read about it on their phone in a few minutes, but newspapers have to wait until the next day. Another advantage is that most online news is free, so people do not need to buy a newspaper every day. Also, people can choose the topics they are interested in, for example sport, technology or business, and they can read news from many different countries. In addition, readers can write comments and share their opinion with other people.

However, online news also have some disadvantages. The biggest problem is fake news. Anyone can write something on the internet or on social media, and many people believe it without checking. This can cause confusion and even danger, for example when false information about health spreads quickly. Moreover, many websites use shocking titles to attract more clicks, so the news is not always serious or accurate. Another disadvantage is that social media shows people only the news which they already agree with, so they do not see other opinions.

In conclusion, getting news online is quick, cheap and convenient, and people have more choice than before. However, there is a big risk of false informations and one-sided news. I think people should read news from reliable websites and always check the facts before they believe or share something.
samples.why: Addresses both sides · relevant ideas with some simple examples, development limited · mechanical linking (Also, In addition, Moreover) · adequate vocabulary, some imprecise choices · agreement and countability errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
Over the last two decades, the internet has overtaken newspapers and television as the main source of news for many people. This shift has made information more accessible than ever before, but it has also created new problems regarding reliability and balance.

One clear advantage of online news is its speed. Breaking stories are reported within minutes and constantly updated, whereas printed newspapers can only report events the following day. Online news is also highly convenient and usually free, since readers can access it on their phones wherever they are. Another benefit is variety: people can compare coverage from many different outlets, including international sources, and focus on topics that interest them. Furthermore, the internet gives ordinary people a voice, as eyewitnesses can share photos and videos of events as they happen, sometimes before professional journalists arrive.

On the other hand, the move online has several drawbacks. The most serious is the spread of misinformation. Unlike established newspapers and broadcasters, which employ editors to check facts, many websites and social media accounts publish claims without any verification, and false stories can go viral before they are corrected. In addition, because many online outlets depend on advertising revenue, they are tempted to use sensational headlines to attract clicks, which can lower the quality of journalism. Algorithms on social media also tend to show users content that matches their existing views, so people may be exposed to only one side of an issue, which can increase division in society.

In conclusion, online news offers speed, convenience and a wide range of perspectives, but it also makes it harder to separate reliable reporting from rumours and can reinforce people's existing beliefs. For this reason, readers need to develop the skills to evaluate the sources they relies on.
samples.why: Both sides clearly presented and extended with relevant support · clear central topic in each paragraph · range of cohesive devices · good collocation (breaking stories, go viral) · mostly error-free, one agreement slip.

samples.text:
The way people consume news has been transformed in a single generation, with websites, apps and social media now replacing the morning paper and the evening bulletin for a large share of the population. This transition has democratised access to information, yet it has also weakened some of the safeguards that traditional media provided.

The advantages are considerable. Online platforms deliver news almost instantaneously, allowing readers to follow developing stories in real time rather than waiting for the next edition or broadcast. Much of this content is free and available on a device most people carry at all times, which has made current affairs accessible to groups who might never have bought a newspaper. The sheer breadth of sources is also valuable: a reader can compare how a single event is covered by outlets in different countries, consult specialist analysis on niche subjects and even see footage captured by eyewitnesses on the ground. In this sense, the internet has diversified the range of voices that shape public debate.

However, the same openness brings serious drawbacks. Because anyone can publish, the traditional filters of editorial oversight and fact-checking are frequently absent, and misleading or entirely fabricated stories can circulate widely before they are challenged. The economic model of much online journalism compounds the problem: revenue depends on clicks, which rewards sensationalism over careful reporting. Perhaps most insidiously, the algorithms that curate news feeds tend to prioritise content that confirms users' existing views, gradually enclosing them in so-called echo chambers and contributing to a more polarised society. The shift has also undermined the finances of many local newspapers, leaving some communities with little independent coverage of local affairs.

In conclusion, online news offers unprecedented speed, accessibility and diversity, but these gains are accompanied by a decline in reliability and a tendency towards polarisation. Its value therefore depends heavily on readers' willingness to seek out trustworthy sources and a range of perspectives.
samples.why: Sufficiently addresses both advantages and disadvantages with well-developed ideas · logical sequencing and skilful cohesion · wide, precise vocabulary (democratised, echo chambers, insidiously) · wide range of error-free structures.
